name: Binary Trees
summary: Allocate, walk and discard millions of perfect binary trees (the Benchmarks Game program, sequential).

spec.description: The Computer Language Benchmarks Game classic. Short-lived trees are built node by node, walked and thrown away while one long-lived tree stays in memory: it measures allocation speed, garbage collector or allocator pressure and recursive pointer chasing.
spec.input: Exactly one argument N made only of ASCII digits (leading zeros allowed), with 0 ≤ N ≤ 21.
spec.output: With minDepth = 4, maxDepth = max(6, N): "stretch tree of depth {maxDepth+1}\t check: {c}", then for depth = 4, 6, …, ≤ maxDepth "{iterations}\t trees of depth {depth}\t check: {sum}" with iterations = 2^(maxDepth − depth + 4), then "long lived tree of depth {maxDepth}\t check: {c}". Every line ends with \n. Exit code 0.
rules: tree(0) is a leaf (no children); tree(d) is a node whose two children are tree(d − 1), built bottom-up recursively. check(node) = 1 for a leaf, 1 + check(left) + check(right) otherwise.

Order: build, check and drop the stretch tree (depth maxDepth + 1); build the long-lived tree (depth maxDepth) and keep it alive while every tree of every iteration depth is built, checked and dropped one at a time; finally check the long-lived tree.

One heap allocation per node where the language has a general-purpose allocator (GC objects, Box, std::unique_ptr, tuples). No memory pools or arenas, no threads. Assembly has no allocator: it carves nodes from its own mmap'd arenas, released after each tree.
Missing or extra arguments, non-digit characters or N > 21: usage message on stderr, nothing on stdout, exit code 1.

benchmarks.name: Depth 10
benchmarks.description: N = 10: 1,360 small trees (~136,000 nodes) — mostly startup plus a short burst of allocation.

benchmarks.name: Depth 16
benchmarks.description: N = 16: 87,376 trees, about 14.6 million nodes allocated, walked and freed next to a 131,071-node long-lived tree — allocator and garbage collector throughput.
